title: Dopamine toolkit: managing baseline, peaks, and motivation (newsletter)
summary: Huberman explains dopamine as the molecule of wanting and motivation, then lists ways to keep baseline healthy (morning sun, tyrosine, avoiding late-night light and melatonin, caffeine) and to manage peaks (random intermittent rewards, subjective control, spotlighting, not stacking stimulants, supplement microspiking).

principles.text: Dopamine drives wanting and motivation, not having; serotonin relates to well-being about what you already have.
principles.quote: The simplest way to think about dopamine is that when our dopamine levels are elevated, we tend to focus our attention on outward goals — the things we want — and we feel motivated to pursue them.

principles.text: View early morning sunlight for 10-30 minutes daily to raise baseline dopamine; a brief cold shower adds to it.
principles.quote: Viewing early morning sunlight** for 10-30 minutes daily.

principles.text: Avoid bright light between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., since it reduces circulating dopamine via the habenula; keep it very dim if needed.
principles.quote: Avoid viewing bright lights between 10 p.m.-4 a.m**.

principles.text: Eat tyrosine-rich foods, avoid melatonin supplements (except for jet lag), and use caffeine (100-400mg) early, not close to sleep.
principles.quote: Tyrosine is an amino acid and a building block of dopamine — a diet rich in tyrosine will sustain your body’s natural dopamine production.

principles.text: Use random intermittent reward timing: celebrate some wins, not every one, and tie winning to the effort process itself.
principles.quote: The key is to **celebrate your wins, but do not celebrate every win**.

principles.text: Don't layer too many dopamine sources (preworkout, music, nootropics, etc.); stacking causes a crash and undermines long-term drive.
principles.quote: But stacking all these dopamine-triggering sources causes a crash afterward, ultimately undermining our longer-term motivation and continued drive.
